question: How deep is the Mariana Trench?

passages.text: How deep is the Mariana Trench? The bottom of the Mariana Trench is about 35,876 feet (10,935 meters) deep, making it deeper than Mount Everest is tall. The deepest part of the ocean is found in the crescent-shaped Mariana Trench, located in the western Pacific Ocean. But what is the deepest point of the Mariana Trench? The Mariana Trench is about 1,580 miles (2,550 kilometers) long and located to the east of the Mariana Islands, which give the trench its name, according to the University of Washington. The deepest spot in the Mariana Trench is a valley called the Challenger Deep, located at the Mariana Trench's southern end, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). According to NOAA, the Challenger Deep extends about 35,876 feet (10,935 meters) below the surface. That makes it about 7,000 feet (2,100 m) deeper than Mount Everest is tall, NOAA noted. NOAA's estimate comes from a 2021 study in the journal Deep Sea Research Part I: Oceanographic Research Papers, based on data from a 2020 voyage. passages.text: How Deep The Mariana Trench Really Is The Mariana Trench is 36,070 feet deep at its deepest point. Converted to miles, this is 6.831 miles deep, which is commonly rounded up to 7 miles in popular science articles. Named after the Mariana Islands to the west of the trench in the Pacific Ocean, this trench was formed by tectonic activity. It is home to sea creatures that have adapted to the intense pressure and darkness of this deep-sea environment. However, only a tiny portion of this trench has been explored by humans. Geography and Geology The Mariana Trench sits at 17.75 N latitude and 142.5 E longitude. It is a 1,580-mile-long by 43-mile-wide geographic formation in the shape of a crescent. It sits at an average of 124 miles to the east of the Mariana Islands. Most of the trench falls within the Mariana Trench Marine National Monument, established by President George W. Bush in January 2009, whose Trench Unit is managed as the Mariana Trench National Wildlife Refuge. It has translucent skin, so thin that its internal organs are visible through it, and no swim bladder, which would collapse at that depth. One of the most recognizable animals from the trench is the black seadevil, which has a bioluminescent lure on the top of its head that it uses to attract prey. Once there, it uses its rows of sharp teeth to catch the prey. This fish lives at depths of 656 feet and beyond, reaching more than 4,900 feet beneath the surface. How much have we seen of the Mariana Trench? The entirety of the Mariana Trench has been mapped using sonar, but much of it remains unexplored. The deep sea in general remains unexplored, with less than 0.001% of it being seen by humans. Sonar itself has only mapped out just under 30% of the seafloor. passages.text: The Mariana Trench is the ocean’s deepest point. The trench runs more than 1,500 miles long and stretches across a Western strip of the Pacific Ocean south of Japan and north of Papua New Guinea. The Mariana Islands are the trench’s namesake, sitting on a piece of the western ridge. At its widest, the Mariana Trench is 44 miles across and could encompass the earth’s largest canyon more than 100 times over. The lowest point in the trench is also the lowest point of the entire ocean, known as the Challenger Deep. We’ll look at the Mariana Trench, uncovering its origins, history, and some of the interesting life forms that call it home. The Challenger Deep The lowest point in the Mariana Trench, the Challenger Deep, is just under 36,000 feet deep. That’s roughly 6.7 miles. You’ll often hear people describe the magnitude of the Challenger Deep by saying “you could fit Mount Everest inside of it.” You could, in fact, fit the 29,032-foot Everest into this pit and have more than a mile left over. The trench is part of a subduction zone, where one plate of the Earth's crust goes under another. In the case of the Mariana Trench, the Pacific plate is going beneath the Philippine plate. The Pacific plate bends as it goes downward, creating a long, deep trench. The western Pacific seafloor dates back to 180 million years ago, making it some of the oldest seafloor on Earth. It was formed initially by lava at ridges. This lava cooled down and turned into dense rock, allowing the seafloor to sink lower, which contributes to the depth of the Mariana Trench. As the trench is not close to any landmasses, it is not filled with sediments from rivers, which would reduce its overall depth. In addition, the Pacific plate is cut into a narrower shape by fault lines along the trench. This allows it to bend downward at a steeper angle than with other subduction zones. In fact, scientists used the deep-learning model EQTransformer to measure seismic activity in this area and discovered there were 1,975 earthquakes in the area in the first half of 2017 alone. Some of these were identified as taking place 31 miles below the surface. What is the deepest point in the Mariana Trench? The deepest point in the trench is Challenger Deep. Despite the name, it actually consists of three seafloor basins or pools at the very bottom of the trench. Currently, it is the lowest point on Earth. The Challenger Deep gets its name from the HMS Challenger, the first boat to chart the area in 1875. It sits on the southern section of the trench, about 200 miles southwest of Guam. The pressure in Challenger Deep is around 16,000 pounds per square inch. This is about 1,000 times more than the pressure at sea level. The water itself is 5% denser than at the surface, and its temperature sits between 34 and 39 degrees Fahrenheit.

passages.text: The Mariana Trench is the deepest oceanic trench on Earth, located in the western Pacific Ocean east of the Mariana Islands. Its deepest point, the Challenger Deep, reaches approximately 10,935 meters (35,876 feet) below sea level. The trench stretches roughly 2,550 kilometers long and averages 69 kilometers wide, forming a crescent-shaped scar on the ocean floor. Introduction The trench was formed by the subduction of the Pacific Plate beneath the smaller Mariana Plate, a process that has been ongoing for millions of years. The extreme depth creates conditions almost inconceivable on the surface: water pressure exceeds 1,000 atmospheres, temperatures hover just above freezing, and perpetual darkness prevails. Yet life exists even here. The Short Answer - Maximum Depth: 10,935 m (35,876 ft) at Challenger Deep - Length: ~2,550 km - Width: ~69 km average - Pressure at Bottom: ~1,086 atmospheres (15,931 psi) The Challenger Deep, named after the HMS Challenger expedition that first surveyed it in 1875, is located at the southern end of the Mariana Trench at approximately 11.3°N, 142.2°E. The exact depth has been refined through multiple measurements: the most precise measurement, by the research vessel DSSV Pressure Drop in 2019, placed the deepest point at 10,935 meters.

passages.text: suggested that microbial life forms thrive within the trench.[8][9] Etymology The Mariana Trench is named after the nearby Mariana Islands,[10] which are named Las Marianas in honor of Spanish Queen Mariana of Austria.[11] The islands are part of the island arc that is formed on an over-riding plate, called the Mariana plate (also named for the islands), on the western side of the trench.[12] Geology The Mariana Trench is part of the Izu–Bonin–Mariana subduction system that forms the boundary between two tectonic plates. In this system, the western edge of one plate, the Pacific plate, is subducted (i.e., thrust) beneath the smaller Mariana plate that lies to the west. Crustal material at the western edge of the Pacific plate is some of the oldest oceanic crust on Earth (up to 170 million years old), and is cooler and denser; hence its great height difference relative to the higher-riding (and younger) Mariana plate. The deepest area at the plate boundary is the Mariana Trench proper.[13] The movement of the Pacific and Mariana plates is also indirectly responsible for the formation of the Mariana Islands. The Challenger Deep was first measured using echo sounding in 1951, and the recorded depth at that time was 35,760 feet. In 2009, a sonar multibeam bathymetry system recorded a depth of 35,994 in Challenger Deep, and that is the current record. The Challenger Deep was first reached by Jaques Piccard and Don Walsh, an oceanographer and Navy Lieutenant, respectively. The two men sunk in for more than five hours in a vessel called The Trieste. They reached the bottom on January 23rd, 1960. Life in The Trench The barren conditions of the ocean at such a depth would seem incompatible with life. Still, scientists have found giant multinucleate unicellular organisms called xenophyophores as well as amphipods, clumps of microbes, and even fish. The Mariana snailfish, for example, is believed to have the deepest habitat of any fish. It exists with no known natural predators and enjoys access to a bounty of invertebrate prey.
